title: Measure of merit (Kern ch. 16)
hookLine: the merit of hearing that the Buddha's life is endless

cards: A phone lights up on the kitchen counter. Three words: the scan's clear. Nothing in the kitchen moves; the kettle is still warming.
And yet the person holding the phone sits down, because the whole afternoon has changed shape. News can do that. It changes nothing you can touch and everything about the day.

The chapter before this one gave its listeners news like that: the Buddha's life is beyond measure, and he is always here. Chapter sixteen, in Kern's numbering, asks what it is worth simply to hear it.

teach.b: First, the word. Merit, punya in Sanskrit, is the Buddhist name for the good an action sets growing, the way a seed keeps working long after it goes into the ground.

You met it in year one, sharing the merit at the end of practice. Buddhists speak of making merit through giving, good conduct and meditation, and of dedicating it to the good of others. Second, the measure.
The Buddha speaks to Maitreya, who, tradition says, will be the next Buddha, and sets two things side by side.
On one side, someone who spends ages beyond counting practicing giving, good conduct, patience, energy and meditation.
On the other, someone who hears that the Tathagata's life is this long and, for a single moment, trusts it.

teach.h: ONE GLAD MOMENT, AGES OF EFFORT.
teach.b: In the sutra's measure, the moment outweighs the ages. Third, why. One reading: the long practices are things done; the moment of trust is a thing seen.
The one who hears isn't adding effort to a pile, but recognizing that what they hoped for is already here. The chapter goes further.
Those who hear and keep this teaching have no need to build stupas or monasteries for him; keeping it is already that offering.
And the place where someone keeps, reads or copies it is to be honored as if the Buddha stood there. Fourth, what this does to merit.
Here it is not a scoreboard. Effort is not wasted, but the door opens by a moment of trust, not by the number of hours.
Glad news, taken in and trusted, is already practice.

how: In schools that center the Lotus Sutra, such as Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren Buddhism, people read, recite and copy the sutra and speak of the merit of faith and joy in hearing it; in a range of Buddhist schools, the merit of a practice is dedicated to the good of others.

o: one moment of trust weighed above ages of effort
a fee paid to a temple in exchange for a blessing
a prize given to the best meditator in a monastery

games.q: measure of merit: tap the pairs.
p: merit: the good an act sets growing
the bodhisattva the Buddha speaks to
outweighed by one moment of trust

s: in this chapter, merit is measured by how many hours you practice
the sutra weighs one moment of trust above ages of effort.
the Buddha says those who keep this teaching need not build stupas or monasteries for him
keeping the teaching is itself the offering, the chapter says.
the place where someone keeps or copies the sutra is to be honored
the chapter says to honor it as if the Buddha stood there.

games.q: you have practiced giving and patience for ages. a stranger hears that the Buddha's life is beyond measure and trusts it for one moment. whose merit does the sutra call greater?
games.why: the chapter weighs the single moment of trust above ages of the long practices: the door opens by trust, not by the pile of hours.

practice: Look back through the last few days for one good thing; small is fine, a friend's message, a plant that bloomed, someone else's good fortune.
Hold it without analyzing it or planning what to do with it, and if gladness comes, let it take up the whole breath. If the mind slides toward a worry, come back to the news.

wordCard.voice: Measure of merit. In the Lotus Sutra, the teaching that one moment of trust outweighs ages of effort. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: merit, the good an action sets growing; in Pali, puñña.

carryVoice: Your line: glad news. A single moment can outweigh the ages. That's today, done.
